# Handball and basketball v2

Measured production fits, a lean (margin, total) model on R-INLA with Stan as reference, and a cutover proposal · four cells: handball and basketball, men and women · prepared 15 November 2026, revised 16 November after an independent check, on branch `feat/hb-bb-v2` · no production path, config or ingest was changed

The handball and basketball models share the football model's structure and, measured, its defects. The home advantage the production fits imply, set against the raw home-minus-away margin, is 1.49 against 0.75 in handball men (×1.98), 1.52 against 0.67 in handball women (×2.26), 4.20 against 3.47 in basketball men (×1.21), 3.86 against 2.37 in basketball women (×1.63). In handball that is the same twofold inflation as in football. A much smaller model does the same job: one net strength per team for the margin, one scoring level per team for the total, a pooled home advantage, all Gaussian, fitted by R-INLA in about 6 seconds per cell on one core (margin and total together; the median over 600 weekly fits, timed on the same shared machine as the production fits, so good for the ratio and not a benchmark), where the production fits took 11 to 56 minutes each under a part-loaded machine. Refitted every week and scored over five seasons (3,930 matches), it is calibrated. On the 338 matches where production's own stored forecasts exist it is better on handball totals; the handball margin and result differences, and every basketball difference, are within noise. Two sport-specific findings matter for the product: regulation-time scores for basketball can be had from the source already in use (99.7 % of stored games), and level scores after regulation are 3.0 times as common in the men's top division as a smooth curve implies.

**The HTML build of this report is local-only and is not in git** (`docs/reports/*.html` is ignored). The branch carries what produces it: the build scripts in `docs/reports/2026-11-15-hb-bb-v2/`, a Markdown rendering written by the same run (`report.md` in that folder, tracked) and a `README.md` with the rebuild command. The result files the scripts read are local too (`/Users/brynjolfurjonsson/.claude-reviews/sports-hb-bb-v2/`); without them the report is rebuilt by rerunning the experiment (appendix, "Reproducing").

## Summary

1.  **The football defects are present.** Home advantage implied by the production fit against the raw home-minus-away margin: handball men 1.49 against 0.75 (×1.98); handball women 1.52 against 0.67 (×2.26); basketball men 4.20 against 3.47 (×1.21); basketball women 3.86 against 2.37 (×1.63). The per-team volatility hierarchies are weakly identified at best (one team's interval for its volatility is about as wide as the whole spread between teams), handball's per-team score sds are indistinguishable, and 31 to 53 % of the sampled innovation slots touch no match. Student-t degrees of freedom: handball men 24, handball women 31, basketball men 13, basketball women 12 (prior median 18), so handball does not ask for heavy tails and basketball asks for a little.
2.  **The home advantage itself is small.** Identified, it is 0.66 and 0.65 goals in handball (men, women) and 3.33 and 2.21 points in basketball, in each case equal to the raw margin within its standard error. The handball figure is about a third of the Bundesliga's 1.87.
3.  **Margin and total can be modelled separately**: their residuals are uncorrelated in every cell. Given the strengths, a handball side's score has 0.49 to 0.60 of the variance a Poisson count would in the league divisions; a Gaussian with a free sd fits, for the women as for the men.
4.  **The ladder attributes the gains.** handball men: removing the states no match touches takes the sampled parameters from 7,972 to 4,656 and the leapfrog steps per iteration from 190 to 127 without moving a score; collapsing the volatility hierarchies changes nothing (home advantage still 1.49); pooling the home effects and freeing their sign takes the home advantage to 0.73 and adds 27 to the leave-one-out density; dropping the Student-t costs 1.2; the identified Gaussian rung has 4,547 parameters at 127 leapfrog steps, against 7,972 at 190 in production; basketball men: collapsing the volatility hierarchies changes nothing (home advantage still 4.20); pooling the home effects and freeing their sign takes the home advantage to 3.26 and adds 5 to the leave-one-out density; dropping the Student-t costs 23.5; the identified Gaussian rung has 6,887 parameters at 127 leapfrog steps, against 9,930 at 446 in production.
5.  **Where v2 is not ahead: women's basketball at the fixed cutoff.** On its 94 held-out matches production has the better win/loss log likelihood (v2 static −0.038 ± 0.019, with the within-season term −0.028 ± 0.014) and the better leave-one-out density (−9,350 against −9,384 and −9,356). On the 67 women's matches with stored forecasts the sign is the other way (+0.054 ± 0.043). Basketball's production fits also beat static v2 on leave-one-out density for the men (−12,946 against −12,974) while losing on the held-out matches. The within-season term and a heavier tail are what production has and static v2 lacks; both are tested above.
6.  **R-INLA reproduces NUTS.** On one identical model, the largest difference in a state's posterior mean is 0.43 posterior sds, the largest difference in a held-out match's expected margin or total is 0.45, and the held-out log scores agree to 0.0026. R-INLA with hyperparameters at their mode, which the walk-forward uses, differs by at most 0.0009. R-INLA is not bit-reproducible between runs: of 48 fits (eight models, 6 runs on the same data), 2 landed on a slightly different optimum (handball men's home advantage 0.653 against 0.659).
7.  **Walk-forward.** 3,930 matches scored over seasons 2023 to 2027 with weekly refits. The predictive spread is calibrated: the standardised margin residual has sd between 0.97 and 1.08 per cell, and between 0.87 and 1.15 in every regular-season phase of every cell. On the 338 matches with a stored production forecast: handball margin +0.043 ± 0.029, total +0.072 ± 0.025, result +0.011 ± 0.021; basketball margin +0.048 ± 0.040, total +0.005 ± 0.021, result +0.005 ± 0.021 (log score per match, v2 minus production, pooled over the sexes). Better on handball totals; handball margin and result within noise; basketball within noise. Margin and total were scored separately; joint (home, away) scores were not evaluated.
8.  **Handball.** The ±0.5 band is the rounded margin, so it stays; what is added is one draw-shift parameter. Men's level scores run above the band (7.3 % against 6.1 % out of sample) but the surplus moves from season to season and the shift has not yet improved the out-of-sample score; women's are calibrated. The possession-informed variance does not beat a free variance and is clearly worse for the women's margin.
9.  **Basketball.** Regulation-time scores exist for 99.7 % of stored games from the source already in use. 7.1 % of men's Bónusdeild games are level after regulation, three times the smooth rate; a tie parameter per division improves the regulation 1X2 score out of sample. Overtime has so far been a coin flip (the favourite won 49 of 97).
10. **Proposal.** v2 on R-INLA for both sports (static for handball, with the within-season term for basketball), basketball on regulation time; swap the engine behind an adapter that keeps the published JSON contract; a four to five week shadow period per sport with a stated gate; store regulation-time scores. Seven decisions are yours.

## Measured and not measured

### Measured

- Production fits at one cutoff with production settings: Handball men, Handball women, Basketball men, Basketball women.
- Ladder rungs fitted with NUTS: Handball men (12 rows); Handball women (6 rows); Basketball men (11 rows); Basketball women (6 rows).
- R-INLA against Stan on one identical model: Handball men, Basketball men.
- Weekly walk-forward of v2 over seasons 2022 to 2027, all four cells: 4,815 matches predicted, 3,930 scored (seasons 2023 on).
- Out-of-sample tests of: the level-score shift (per sex, per division, by closeness), four variance forms including the possession-informed one, a Student-t predictive, the overtime model.
- Comparison with production's stored forecasts on 338 matches and with the Lengjan line where odds exist.
- Regulation-time scores for 3,272 of 3,283 stored basketball games.
- Residual diagnostics by division, season and sex.
- Run-to-run reproducibility of the R-INLA plug-in fits: 6 runs of the eight fits on the same data.

### Not measured

- A walk-forward of the within-season AR(1) for handball (dropped from the queue: the fixed-cutoff fit shows nothing for it to find).
- Weekly correlations other than 0.98 for the within-season term in the walk-forward (0.90 and 0.95 were only checked at the fixed cutoff).
- Production in a walk-forward: one production fit takes tens of minutes, so production is represented by its fixed-cutoff fit and by the forecasts it actually stored (April to May and September to November 2026 only).
- Joint (home, away) score distributions. The parity-respecting sampler `v2_sample_scores()` exists and is unit-tested (`R/v2-margin-total-predict.R`), but the walk-forward scored margin and total as two separate whole-number distributions, so joint scores were not evaluated.
- Clean wall-clock benchmarks: every time was taken on a shared machine, the R-INLA fit times included.
- The full ladder for the women's cells (production and the final model only, by agreement with the scheduling session).
- The published JSON built end to end from a v2 fit: the adapter's algebra is tested, the wiring into `fit_league()` is proposed, not built.
- A league-table (season simulation) comparison between the engines.
- Genius Sports LiveStats as a second source of period scores: not needed, not tried.
- Whether the market beats the model: too few priced matches (65 handball, 20 basketball).

## Production fits, measured

Each production Stan model was fitted once at a fixed cutoff, 31 January 2026, with production's sampler settings (4 chains, 1,000 warm-up and 1,000 draws, `adapt_delta` 0.95, tree depth 10, CmdStan 2.38.0, the version CI pins). The matches of 1 February to 31 May 2026 were held out; forfeits are excluded from training, as production does, and from every scored set.

| Cell | Training matches | Teams | Held out (by division) | Sampled parameters | Innovation slots no match touches | Divergences | Leapfrog steps per iteration | Largest R-hat | Smallest bulk ESS (parameter) | Wall time |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Handball men | 1,097 | 36 | 103 (G66 41, OD 42, PO 20) | 7,972 | 43 % | 33 | 190 | 1.012 | 300 (`scale_sigma_def`) | 13.1 min |
| Handball women | 855 | 25 | 64 (G66 24, OD 24, PO 16) | 5,291 | 33 % | 0 | 159 | 1.012 | 601 (`scale_sigma_def`) | 10.5 min |
| Basketball men | 1,690 | 28 | 130 (1D 64, BD 66) | 9,930 | 31 % | 0 | 446 | 1.011 | 529 (`scale_sigma_off`) | 56.3 min |
| Basketball women | 1,224 | 30 | 94 (1D 37, BD 57) | 10,638 | 53 % | 0 | 319 | 1.010 | 425 (`scale_sigma_off`) | 44.1 min |

"Innovation slots no match touches" is a property of the data layout: the model has one state per team per appearance index up to the league maximum, so a team with a short history carries slots that only the prior sees. Wall times were taken inside the shared machine limiter (two, later three, 4-core jobs at once on 8 performance cores), usually with one or two sibling fits running: good for ratios, not benchmarks. The handball men fit was first run before the limiter existed, at two to three times oversubscription; it was run again inside a slot with the same seed, gave identical results, and that second run is the time shown.

Per the owner's standing rule, the aggregate is broken down before anything is redesigned: the inflation is present in every division measured, largest where the raw advantage is smallest.

*Figure (drawn in the HTML build only).* Home advantage in score units (goals for handball, points for basketball). A missing production bar means that cell's production fit had not finished. The v2 bar is the league home advantage of the identified model fitted to all data.

**Reading the table.** Home advantage is overstated because each team has its own attack and defence home effect, each forced to be non-negative with a half-normal(0, 10) prior and no pooling. In handball men the typical team's attack home effect has posterior sd 0.57 around a mean of 0.85: the estimates are noise-dominated, the zero bound pushes every one of them upward, and the error cannot average out. The intercept ridge that the football review found (scoring level traded against the two home means) is truncated by the same bounds instead of being removed, which is why the correlations in the table are weak here; the ladder below shows it reappear the moment the bounds are lifted. The volatility hierarchies are weakly identified at best: in handball men the scale parameters' posteriors match the exponential(2) prior, and in every cell one team's interval for its own random-walk sd is about as wide as the whole spread between teams. The Student-t degrees of freedom sit above their prior in handball, so those data are not asking for heavy tails; in basketball they sit a little below it.

Margin is home minus away, total is home plus away. "Score variance / mean" is the Pearson dispersion of each side's score around its fitted mean: 1 would be Poisson (stored as `pearson_poisson` in `out/descriptives.rds`, `[[cell]]$disp`). Handball's PO rows are the 2026 play-offs only (16 and 20 matches).

**Margin and total are uncorrelated** once strengths are in: every cell is within a few hundredths of zero. That is the condition under which the two can be modelled separately, and it holds. **Handball scores are under-dispersed**: the variance of a side's score is 0.49 to 0.60 of its mean in the league divisions, for women as for men (0.73 and 0.76 in the two small play-off samples), so a Poisson model would be badly over-dispersed and a free Gaussian variance is the honest choice. **Tails are close to Gaussian** in handball. Basketball margins are somewhat heavier-tailed, and women's 1. deild markedly so, with a few very large margins; the walk-forward tests whether a heavier-tailed predictive pays.

The margin is slightly more variable, and the favourite wins by slightly more than a straight line predicts, when the teams are far apart. The effect is real but small next to the match-to-match noise; whether modelling it pays is tested out of sample below, and it does not.

## The ladder

Each rung changes one thing, so each gain is attributable. All rungs are fitted with NUTS at the same cutoff and settings as production. At the request of the session that scheduled the machine, the full ladder was run for the two men's cells; the women's cells have the production fit and the final model.

### Reading the handball men ladder

- **R1** keeps production's model and removes only the states no match touches: 4,656 sampled parameters instead of 7,972, 127 leapfrog steps per iteration instead of 190, held-out scores unchanged (margin 0.000 ± 0.001).
- **R2** replaces the per-team volatility hierarchies and the per-team score sds by single values: 4,545 parameters and 127 leapfrog steps per iteration, leave-one-out −6,262.6 against −6,261.1. The home advantage is still 1.49: it is not the hierarchies that inflate it.
- **R3** pools the home effects and lets them take either sign: the home advantage falls from 1.49 to 0.73 (raw margin 0.75), leave-one-out rises to −6,235.8 and the held-out margin log score by +0.039 ± 0.018. The ridge that the bounds were hiding appears: the scoring level's posterior sd goes from 0.65 to 3.46, its correlation with the mean attack home effect is −0.98, and NUTS needs 255 leapfrog steps per iteration.
- **R4** removes the ridge (one league home advantage, team deviations around zero): the level's sd returns to 0.66, leapfrog steps to 127, the smallest effective sample size is 1,104, the home advantage is 0.73.
- **R5** drops the Student-t (fitted degrees of freedom in R4: 23): leave-one-out −6,238.1 against −6,236.8, held-out margin −0.003 ± 0.007 and total +0.002 ± 0.006. That is the measure of what the heavy tail is worth.
- **v2** rotates attack and defence into net strength and scoring level, adds the club level and the season-boundary AR(1) and drops the appearance-indexed random walk: 563 sampled parameters, leave-one-out −6,228.0, held-out margin −0.001 ± 0.006 and total +0.012 ± 0.016 against R5.

### Reading the basketball men ladder

The home advantage is still 4.20: it is not the hierarchies that inflate it.

## The v2 model

Margin = home score minus away score, total = home plus away. The two are modelled separately because their residuals are uncorrelated.

margin ~ Normal( hfa + ha\[home\] + s\[home\] - s\[away\] ,  sigma_m )\
total  ~ Normal( level\[division, season\] + p\[home\] + p\[away\] ,  sigma_t )\
\
s\[team, date\] = b\[team\] + u\[team, season\] (+ w\[team-season, week\])      net strength\
p\[team, date\] = b'\[team\] + u'\[team, season\] (+ w'\[team-season, week\])   contribution to the total\
\
b ~ Normal(0, sigma_b)                    club level, constant over the data\
u\[season + 1\] = rho \* u\[season\] + noise   season level, AR(1) across seasons, sd sigma_u\
w                                         within-season movement (three forms tested)\
ha ~ Normal(0, sigma_ha)                  team deviation from the league home advantage\
level\[division, .\]                        random walk over seasons, one path per division

Nothing in it is forced to have a sign, the league home advantage is one number, and there is one row type per model, so there is no ridge to separate with priors. Every piece is Gaussian, which makes R-INLA's Laplace step exact; the only approximation left is the numerical integration over six hyperparameters per model.

### Each parameter's data story

| Parameter | What in the game it stands for | Prior |
|----|----|----|
| `hfa` | Playing at home is worth a fixed number of goals or points on average: travel, the hall, the crowd, referees. One number per sex, free to take either sign. | normal(0, 5) goals / normal(0, 10) points |
| `sigma_m`, `sigma_t` | What is left of a match once strengths are known: shooting luck, the day's form, refereeing. One sd for the margin and one for the total, because the data show no difference between teams and margin and total do not co-vary. | sd above 15 / 20 goals or 30 / 40 points with probability 1 % |
| `b`, `sigma_b` | Some clubs are big and some are small for reasons that outlast any roster: budget, youth system, town. This is the level a club returns to. | sd above 10 goals / 25 points with probability 1 % |
| `u`, `sigma_u`, `rho` | Each summer the roster changes (imports in basketball, players leaving for clubs abroad in handball), so a club's strength in a season departs from its long-run level, and part of that departure carries into the next season. `rho` is the share that carries over. | sd above 8 goals / 20 points with probability 1 %; `rho` centred on 0.7, 95 % within 0.13 to 0.92 |
| `w`, `sigma_w` | Injuries, a mid-season signing, a coach finding a system: strength can drift inside a season. Tested as a weekly random walk and as a slow AR(1) around the season level. | random walk: sd above 1 goal / 2.5 points per week with probability 1 % |
| `ha`, `sigma_ha` | Some halls are harder to visit than others. Team deviations from the league home advantage, shrunk hard because a team has about eleven home matches a season. | sd above 3 goals / 6 points with probability 1 % |
| `level`, `sigma_season` | Scoring levels move with rules and style (men's Olísdeild has gone from 53 to 66 goals a match between seasons 2021 and 2027). A random walk over seasons, one path per division. | step sd above 5 goals / 10 points with probability 1 % |

Every sd has an exponential prior stated as an upper bound it exceeds with probability 1 % (R-INLA's PC prior; the same density in Stan). The bounds are several times the size each quantity is expected to take, so the data decide.

Median \[5 %, 95 %\], R-INLA with hyperparameters at their mode for the latent field. Home advantage is the posterior mean. The handball home advantage, about two thirds of a goal for both sexes, is far below the 1.87 goals reported for the German Bundesliga; it equals the raw home-minus-away margin in these leagues.

Team deviations from the league home advantage are small in handball (sd 0.2 and 0.4 goals) and largest in women's basketball (2.3 points, against 1.0 for the men): there the hall matters by team, as the NBA literature found. In women's basketball the data cannot say sharply how much of the spread between teams is club level and how much is season level (wide intervals for both).

## R-INLA against Stan, like for like

One identical model per comparison: v2 with the within-season AR(1) (the richer of the two candidate forms), the same data, the same priors, fitted with NUTS and with R-INLA.

| Model | Largest hyperparameter difference, in posterior sds | States: largest mean difference (sds) / sd ratio | Held-out predictor: largest mean difference / sd ratio | Held-out log score: Stan / INLA full / INLA plug-in | Leave-one-out: Stan PSIS / INLA CPO | Stan | R-INLA time: full / plug-in |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Handball men, margin | 0.25 | 0.133 / 0.931 | 0.116 / 1.029 | −3.0395 / −3.0410 / −3.0402 | −3,320.7 / −3,320.1 | 5,119 params, 0 div., 63 leapfrog | 6 s / 4 s |
| Handball men, total | 0.65 | 0.221 / 0.996 | 0.136 / 1.019 | −3.4521 / −3.4494 / −3.4513 | −3,666.2 / −3,665.6 | 5,094 params, 0 div., 94 leapfrog | 7 s / 6 s |
| Basketball men, margin | 0.32 | 0.190 / 0.984 | 0.386 / 0.981 | −4.0520 / −4.0534 / −4.0529 | −6,832.3 / −6,831.1 | 5,711 params, 0 div., 191 leapfrog | 9 s / 7 s |
| Basketball men, total | 0.68 | 0.433 / 0.990 | 0.448 / 1.013 | −4.2555 / −4.2558 / −4.2554 | −7,305.2 / −7,303.5 | 5,694 params, 0 div., 95 leapfrog | 15 s / 7 s |

"sd ratio" is R-INLA's posterior sd over Stan's, median over states or matches. "Plug-in" fixes the hyperparameters at their mode, which is what the walk-forward uses. R-INLA times are single-core wall times on a shared machine.

**Predictions agree.** Across the 4 comparisons the largest difference in a held-out match's expected margin or total is 0.45 goals or points, the held-out log scores differ by at most 0.0026 per match, and the two leave-one-out estimates by at most 1.7 in total. **What differs is how weakly identified variance is split.** The largest hyperparameter difference is 0.68 posterior sds (`sd: b` in the basketball men total model: Stan 1.88, R-INLA 2.77). In the total models the data cannot say sharply how much of a team's scoring level is club, season or within-season, the posterior of those sds is wide and skewed, and R-INLA's integration grid (26 to 45 points) describes it more narrowly than NUTS does. The sum of the three, which is what a forecast uses, is the same. The Stan reference itself is the weaker side on precision here: its smallest effective sample size is 142, against R-hat up to 1.024.

## Handball: draws and the variance question

### A principled draw probability

Scores are whole numbers and the model's margin is continuous. Rounding the continuous margin to the nearest whole number gives P(draw) = P(\|margin\| \< 0.5), which is exactly production's ±0.5 band. So the band is not wrong in itself. What it cannot do is say that level scores are more or less common than a smooth curve implies. The v2 prediction layer adds one number for that: a shift of the draw probability on the logit scale, with every other margin keeping its relative share. It is estimated from the data per sex, and can be estimated per division.

| Cell | Division | Matches | Level scores | Observed | Rounded Gaussian (the band) | With one shift per sex | With a shift per division |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Handball men | all | 926 | 68 | 7.34 % | 6.14 % | 8.58 % | 8.80 % |
| Handball men | G66 | 382 | 24 | 6.28 % | 5.88 % | 8.23 % | 6.06 % |
| Handball men | OD | 524 | 44 | 8.40 % | 6.27 % | 8.76 % | 10.74 % |
| Handball men | PO | 20 | 0 | 0.00 % | 7.35 % | 10.57 % | 10.57 % |
| Handball women | all | 707 | 34 | 4.81 % | 4.46 % | 4.35 % | 4.40 % |
| Handball women | G66 | 335 | 15 | 4.48 % | 4.07 % | 3.96 % | 4.22 % |
| Handball women | OD | 356 | 19 | 5.34 % | 4.74 % | 4.59 % | 4.45 % |
| Handball women | PO | 16 | 0 | 0.00 % | 6.26 % | 7.03 % | 7.03 % |

Out of sample: seasons 2023 to 2027 of the weekly walk-forward; each season's shift was estimated on the earlier seasons only.

**Men.** Level scores are more common than the band predicts: 7.3 % observed against 6.1 % out of sample, and on all data the shift is 0.30 (se 0.10) on the logit scale, about 35 % more draws. Broken down by division, the surplus is in Olísdeild (shift 0.46 on the seasons before 2027) and absent in Grill 66 (−0.03). It is not stable enough to pay yet: the share of level scores in Olísdeild swings from season to season, the shift estimated on earlier seasons overshoots the later ones, and the out-of-sample W/D/L log likelihood changes by −0.0007 ± 0.0031 with one shift and −0.0026 ± 0.0040 with a shift per division. **Women.** The band is calibrated as it stands: 4.8 % observed against 4.5 %, shift 0.09 (se 0.14).

| 0.2 to 0.4 | 164 | 11.0 % | 7.6 % | 10.6 % | 99 | 11.1 % | 6.3 % | 6.3 % |

Production's draw probability is the share of its posterior draws with \|margin\| at most 0.5. These samples are small; the September audit's 5.5 % predicted against 4.6 % observed was on a different sample.

### Possession-informed variance against a free variance

The literature describes handball goals as binomial counts: about 50 to 60 attacks per side at about 50 % efficiency, with both sides having the same number of attacks. That gives a variance for the margin and the total that follows from the expected scores, with two parameters (attacks per side and the variance of that number) in place of two free sds. The test: fit each variance form on the walk-forward predictions of earlier seasons, score the next season, compare with the free constant variance.

| Variance form | Men: margin | Men: total | Women: margin | Women: total |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Free variance, rescaled on past errors | +0.0029 ± 0.0047 | −0.0018 ± 0.0015 | −0.0081 ± 0.0051 | −0.0031 ± 0.0019 |
| Variance grows with the mismatch (margin) / the expected total | +0.0024 ± 0.0046 | −0.0022 ± 0.0022 | −0.0098 ± 0.0051 | −0.0046 ± 0.0021 |
| One variance per division | +0.0048 ± 0.0059 | −0.0003 ± 0.0027 | +0.0016 ± 0.0067 | −0.0056 ± 0.0024 |
| Possession-informed (binomial with shared attacks) | +0.0004 ± 0.0027 | −0.0017 ± 0.0020 | −0.0301 ± 0.0076 | −0.0059 ± 0.0038 |
| Student-t with fitted degrees of freedom | +0.0016 ± 0.0014 | +0.0019 ± 0.0025 | +0.0039 ± 0.0028 | 0.0000 ± 0.0005 |

Change in the out-of-sample integer log score per match against the plain model (one free sd for the margin, one for the total), with its match-clustered standard error. Positive is better. Men n = 926, women n = 707.

Nothing beats the free variance. The possession-informed form is no better for men and clearly worse for the women's margin (−0.0301 ± 0.0076), the cells the literature disagrees about. The scores do look binomial in one respect: each side's variance is close to that of a binomial with 55 attacks in Olísdeild (ratio 1.07 men, 1.02 women; 1.24 and 1.17 in Grill 66). But the possession form ties the margin variance and the total variance together through its two parameters, and two free sds fit both better. A Student-t with fitted degrees of freedom (28 for the men's margin, 15 for the women's) changes the score by less than its standard error. **Handball keeps a Gaussian with one free sd for the margin and one for the total.**

## Basketball: regulation time

### The data exist, in the source already in use

The Baskethotel results export that the production ingest reads has a game id in its first column, which the parser drops. Baskethotel's game-card widget (number 400 in its `api.js`, the same widget kki.is embeds) returns that game's four quarter scores. One request per game: 3,286 cards were fetched once, 0.35 s apart, into the scratch folder; the production ingest was not touched. The card always lists four quarters, also for overtime games, so regulation time is the quarter sum and an overtime game is a level quarter sum with a final score above it. Genius Sports LiveStats was not needed and was not tried.

| League | Stored played games | With a regulation-time score | Share | Went to overtime | Share of those |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Women, 1. deild | 633 | 629 | 99.4 % | 16 | 2.5 % |
| Women, Bónusdeild | 747 | 745 | 99.7 % | 17 | 2.3 % |
| Men, 1. deild | 899 | 894 | 99.4 % | 34 | 3.8 % |
| Men, Bónusdeild | 1,004 | 1,004 | 100.0 % | 71 | 7.1 % |

Seasons 2021 to 2027. All 3,283 stored games matched a card. The 11 without a usable regulation score are 7 walkovers, 3 cards with no quarter block and 1 whose quarters contradict the recorded final.

*Figure (drawn in the HTML build only).* Basketball men, regulation-time margin, 1,335 walk-forward predictions. Level after regulation: 5.5 % of games against 2.3 % under the smooth curve. Margins of one or two points either way are not depleted to pay for it. The usual explanation is end-game play: the trailing side fouls and shoots threes until the score is level or the game is gone.

### Tie inflation and the overtime model

| Cell | Division | Games | Level after regulation | Observed | Rounded Gaussian | With one shift per sex | With a shift per division |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Basketball men | all | 1,335 | 73 | 5.47 % | 2.29 % | 6.59 % | 6.45 % |
| Basketball men | 1D | 651 | 24 | 3.69 % | 2.20 % | 6.31 % | 4.19 % |
| Basketball men | BD | 684 | 49 | 7.16 % | 2.38 % | 6.84 % | 8.60 % |
| Basketball women | all | 962 | 24 | 2.49 % | 1.80 % | 2.01 % | 1.92 % |
| Basketball women | 1D | 404 | 11 | 2.72 % | 1.44 % | 1.56 % | 1.83 % |
| Basketball women | BD | 558 | 13 | 2.33 % | 2.06 % | 2.32 % | 1.98 % |

Out of sample, seasons 2023 to 2027; each season's shift estimated on earlier seasons.

**Men.** The tie parameter is needed and it differs by division: shift 1.23 in Bónusdeild (about 3.4 times the smooth rate) and 0.65 in 1. deild. It improves the out-of-sample regulation 1X2 log likelihood by +0.0166 ± 0.0072 per game and the regulation-margin log score by the same amount. **Women.** A small surplus (2.5 % against 1.8 %), shift 0.26, no measurable gain yet (+0.0003 ± 0.0007). **Overtime** is modelled as a short continuation of the same game: a five-minute period is one eighth of regulation, so its margin has one eighth of the mean and of the variance, and a level overtime is replayed. On the 97 overtime games in the scored seasons the home side won 53 and the pre-match favourite 49 (51 %); the continuation model expected the favourite to win 57 %, and its log likelihood is −0.697 against −0.693 for a coin flip. So in these leagues overtime has so far been a coin flip, unlike the NBA; the continuation model is kept because it costs nothing and tends to the coin flip for evenly matched teams, but the evidence does not yet support it over 50 : 50.

### Does training on regulation time cost anything for the final result?

| Cell | Games | Final-result log likelihood: final-score model / regulation + overtime | Difference | Final-margin log score: final-score model / regulation + overtime | Difference |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Basketball men | 1,335 | −0.5799 / −0.5795 | +0.0004 ± 0.0006 | −4.0854 / −4.0546 | +0.0308 ± 0.0023 |
| Basketball women | 962 | −0.4931 / −0.4937 | −0.0006 ± 0.0006 | −4.2112 / −4.1910 | +0.0202 ± 0.0013 |

Same matches, both walk-forwards. The final-score model is the same v2 model trained on final scores, with the home side winning when the continuous margin is positive.

One model trained on regulation-time scores serves both products: the regulation 1X2 the bookmaker settles on, and the final result the league table needs, through the tie probability and overtime.

**Tails: is a Student-t worth its cost?** Basketball margins are a little heavier-tailed than Gaussian, most in women's 1. deild. In the ladder, replacing the Student-t by a Gaussian costs the men's fit 24 of leave-one-out density (handball: about 1) and changes no held-out score. In the walk-forward, a Student-t predictive with the same sd and fitted degrees of freedom (8 men, 13 women) improves the regulation-margin log score by +0.0108 ± 0.0040 for men and +0.0064 ± 0.0045 for women, and leaves the result probabilities where they were (men: regulation 1X2 −0.0009 ± 0.0011, final result −0.0003 ± 0.0009; women: −0.0006 ± 0.0005 and −0.0006 ± 0.0005). Variance by division or by mismatch does nothing (largest change +0.0093 ± 0.0090). So the heavier tail sharpens the margin distribution a little and changes no win probability. It is not worth giving up the exact Gaussian fit for; the proposal keeps the Gaussian in the engine and offers the Student-t as a prediction-layer setting for the basketball margin distribution.

## Leak-free walk-forward

For each cell, the model was refitted at every weekly cutoff from the start of season 2022 to 14 November 2026 on the results dated up to the cutoff (production's training filter, forfeits dropped) and asked for the matches of the following seven days. Hyperparameters are re-estimated at every cutoff. Season 2022 is used only to fit the second-stage quantities; scores are for seasons 2023 to 2027. The model is the static form of v2 fitted with R-INLA (hyperparameters at their mode); basketball is trained on regulation-time scores. Margin and total are scored as two separate whole-number distributions. The joint (home, away) score distribution was not scored: the parity-respecting sampler for it exists and is unit-tested (`v2_sample_scores()` in `R/v2-margin-total-predict.R`), but no walk-forward score in this report uses it.

Phases are weeks of the regular season; a basketball play-off match is one of a pair that meets at least three times within three weeks, handball's are its PO division. The mean standardised margin residual is from the home side's view. The predictive sd is widest in the first six weeks because the new season's level is still uncertain: that is the season-boundary term at work.

The spread of the standardised residuals stays close to 1 in every phase, including the last six weeks and the play-offs. If team strength drifted inside a season in a way the static model misses, the late-season residuals would be over-dispersed; they are not, in either sport. This is the check asked for before dropping the within-season term for basketball, where mid-season import changes are the obvious worry.

### Does a within-season term earn its place?

| Cell | Within-season sd (margin model) | Season-level sd | Match sd | Leave-one-out gain from the within-season term | Held-out matches | Held-out margin log score: AR(1) − static | Held-out result log likelihood |

| Handball men | 0.42 \[0.09, 1.21\] | 1.70 \[1.07, 2.90\] | 4.77 \[4.60, 4.96\] | +1.8 | 103 | −0.001 ± 0.002 | +0.001 ± 0.002 |
| Handball women | 1.15 \[0.38, 2.63\] | 4.00 \[2.62, 6.53\] | 5.09 \[4.85, 5.35\] | +2.1 | 64 | −0.010 ± 0.005 | −0.004 ± 0.003 |
| Basketball men | 5.01 \[3.73, 6.86\] | 4.30 \[2.27, 8.17\] | 13.02 \[12.60, 13.45\] | +11.1 | 130 | −0.005 ± 0.008 | +0.002 ± 0.007 |
| Basketball women | 6.60 \[4.96, 8.47\] | 12.11 \[7.97, 18.96\] | 13.27 \[12.76, 13.84\] | +28.0 | 94 | +0.022 ± 0.014 | +0.010 ± 0.010 |

Fixed cutoff 31 January 2026, R-INLA with full hyperparameter integration. The within-season term is a weekly AR(1) around the season level with weekly correlation 0.98; its sd is the size of a team's typical departure from its season level. Median \[5 %, 95 %\].

In handball the within-season sd is half a goal (men) to one goal (women) against a match sd near five, and the term buys nothing. In basketball it is five to seven points, about half the match sd: teams do move within a season, as the import changes would suggest. Whether tracking that movement improves forecasts is what the walk-forward tests.

The weekly correlation of the within-season term is fixed, not estimated, and the data cannot tell 0.90 from 0.98: for the basketball margin model the leave-one-out density stays within −6,827.7 to −6,827.4 (men) and −4,992.0 to −4,991.3 (women) across 0.90, 0.95 and 0.98, and the held-out margin log score within −4.053 to −4.048 and −4.146 to −4.133.

| Basketball men | 96 | +0.0222 ± 0.0364 | +0.0032 ± 0.0226 | −0.0292 ± 0.0196 | 4.50 / 3.74 / 2.22 | 14.93 / 15.17 | 18.54 / 18.05 |

| **Handball, both sexes** | 175 | +0.0429 ± 0.0290 | +0.0725 ± 0.0249 | +0.0113 ± 0.0209 |  |  |  |
| **Basketball, both sexes** | 163 | +0.0477 ± 0.0399 | +0.0049 ± 0.0215 | +0.0050 ± 0.0211 |  |  |  |

Production's forecast is the newest archived fit dated strictly before the match (median lead two to three days); v2's cutoff is up to seven days before the match, so v2 is the one working with older information. The stored forecasts cover late April to May 2026 and September to November 2026. Basketball is scored on the final result; v2 reaches it from its regulation-time model through the tie probability and overtime. Positive differences favour v2.

**What this supports.** One difference is clear: the handball total (2.9 standard errors). The handball margin (1.5 standard errors) and result (0.5) point the same way and are within noise. No basketball difference, per cell or pooled, is larger than 1.5 standard errors: basketball is level within noise. So against production's stored forecasts v2 is better on handball totals, and not shown to be better or worse on anything else.

In handball production expects the home side to win by 2.14 goals on average over these matches; v2 expects 0.80 and the result was 0.75. That is the home-advantage inflation showing up in the published numbers.

### Against the Lengjan line

| Cell | Priced matches | Period | Market 1X2 log likelihood | v2 | v2 − market | Where production's forecast exists: market / production / v2 |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Handball men | 65 | 04 Mar 2026 to 13 Nov 2026 | −0.712 | −0.698 | +0.0145 ± 0.0244 | n = 41: −0.650 / −0.602 / −0.601 |
| Basketball men | 10 | 29 Apr 2026 to 18 May 2026 | −0.768 | −0.783 | −0.0146 ± 0.0607 | n = 10: −0.768 / −0.798 / −0.783 |
| Basketball women | 10 | 04 Mar 2026 to 17 May 2026 | −0.909 | −0.979 | −0.0699 ± 0.1087 | n = 6: −0.818 / −0.836 / −0.749 |

Proportionally de-vigged 1X2, last scrape on or before match day. Handball is full time; basketball is regulation time, where production has no draw probability of its own, so its column uses the ±0.5 band. Odds exist for few matches: the handball men's sample is small and the basketball samples are too small to read.

Compute: 600 weekly cutoffs, two R-INLA fits each (margin and total), median 6.5 s per cutoff for both fits together, single core per cell, four cells side by side inside one slot of the shared limiter while a sibling session's job held the other slot. Like every time in this report it was taken on a shared machine: good for the ratio to the production fits, not a benchmark.

## Cutover proposal

This is a proposal. Nothing below has been done to the production path; each step that would alter live fits or published output is listed under [Your decisions](#your-decisions).

### Recommended model

### Handball, men and women

- v2 **static** form (strength constant within a season), margin and total, fitted with R-INLA on final scores.
- Gaussian, one free sd for the margin and one for the total. No possession-informed variance, no Student-t.
- Prediction layer: whole-number scores with margin and total on the same parity; draw = level score; a draw shift per sex, set to zero for women and, for men, either zero or a shrunk value (a decision below). The joint sampler is built and unit-tested; the walk-forward scored margin and total separately, so joint scores are not yet evaluated.

### Basketball, men and women

- The same model **with the within-season AR(1)**, trained on **regulation-time** scores.
- Tie shift per division for men, one small shift (or none) for women.
- Final result = regulation result, or overtime when level; overtime as a five-minute continuation (which the data so far cannot tell from a coin flip).
- Both regulation-time and final-result probabilities come out of one fit.

Within-season movement: handball does not need it (within-season sd half a goal to one goal, no gain). In basketball the fitted within-season sd is five to seven points and leave-one-out improves by 11 (men) and 28 (women). Over 1,211 walk-forward matches (seasons 2025 to 2027, both sexes) the AR(1) form changes the margin log score by +0.0025 ± 0.0025, the total by +0.0042 ± 0.0020 and the regulation 1X2 log likelihood by +0.0019 ± 0.0017 per match against the static form. The gain sits in 1. deild (549 matches: margin +0.0103 ± 0.0040, total +0.0057 ± 0.0028, 1X2 +0.0055 ± 0.0027) and is nil in Bónusdeild. It is small, never negative when pooled, and costs about ten more seconds of fitting (timed on the shared machine), so the term is kept for basketball; the static form is the fallback. Stan stays in the repository as the reference: the same v2 model in `docs/reports/2026-11-15-hb-bb-v2/stan/v2_margin.stan` and `v2_total.stan`, to be run weekly during the shadow period.

### Engine risks found on the way

- **Starting values.** From R-INLA's default starting precision (an sd of 0.14) the optimiser settled, for men's basketball totals, in a mode with the team effects switched off: a fit that converges and is wrong. `fit_v2_inla()` starts every sd at a fifth of its prior bound, and the proposed diagnostics gate checks that no sd sits at a bound.
- **Constraints are what cost time.** A within-season random walk that sums to zero needs one linear constraint per team-season (over a hundred), and R-INLA then takes 40 to 60 s per fit against 5 s for the static form. The AR(1) form needs none and takes about 15 s. All three were timed on the shared machine: ratios, not benchmarks.
- **Weakly identified variances.** R-INLA's hyperparameter posterior is narrower than NUTS's where the data cannot separate club, season and within-season variance. Forecasts are unaffected; published interval widths for individual team strengths are within a few per cent at the median but differ more for some teams.
- **NUTS has its own trouble with this model.** The season walk of the total model has six steps; in its centred form NUTS produced up to 75 divergences, and it was re-parameterised. R-INLA integrates that variance numerically and has no such failure.
- **Priors can be dropped silently.** R-INLA ignores a hyperparameter specification it cannot read from the model term and fits with its defaults, without a warning (found the same night by the national-team session). `fit_v2_inla()` was checked against the fitted object: every prior, starting value and fixed value is the one stated, and a test now asserts it.
- **Not bit-reproducible between runs.** The eight plug-in fits behind [What the data ask of the likelihood](#what-the-data-ask-of-the-likelihood) were run 6 times in separate R processes on the same data (the original run, the rerun that stored the dispersion table, and four repeats). 46 of the 48 results were bit-identical with the most frequent one; 2 were not, each in a different run: the margin model for handball men (fitted values up to 0.06 goals from the usual result; home advantage 0.653 against 0.659, with a posterior sd of 0.15; the median of the club-level sd 5.06 against 5.09) and the total model for basketball women (fitted values up to 0.11 points from the usual result; the median of the sd of the division level's walk over seasons 3.18 against 3.53). The cause was not investigated. The shifts are a small fraction of a posterior sd, but they mean that a refit on unchanged data can move a published number in the second decimal, which the proposed gate on the change from yesterday's fit has to allow for, and that a rerun of the walk-forward need not reproduce its scores to the last digit. The stored `descriptives.rds` is a run in which every fit is the most frequent result.
- **Installation.** R-INLA is not on CRAN and ships its own binary; the version should be pinned in CI as CmdStan is.

### Shadow period

1.  **Shadow fits.** A separate workflow (or the local machine) fits v2 daily for the four cells and writes to its own tree, for example `data/shadow/`, which neither decide nor publish reads. Nothing on the site changes.
2.  **Weekly scorecard.** The comparison in this report, rerun on the matches played since the shadow began: margin and total log scores, result log likelihood, mean expected margin against observed, draw and overtime calibration, against production's forecast and the Lengjan line where one exists.
3.  **Reference check.** Once a week the same v2 model is fitted with NUTS and compared with that day's R-INLA fit (states and held-out predictions, as in the validation section).
4.  **Gate, per sport.** At least 150 scored matches in shadow; pooled margin and total log scores not worse than production by more than one standard error; mean expected home margin within one standard error of the observed margin; published JSON built from v2 passes `validate-publish` and a side-by-side review of one cell on the site's staging build.
5.  **Cutover.** Flip the engine for handball first, which needs no new data. Basketball follows once regulation-time scores are in `results`. Rollback is flipping the key back; the Stan path is untouched.

In season the four cells play roughly 35 to 45 matches a week between them, so the gate is about four to five weeks of shadow per sport.

### The data decision for basketball

Recommended: store regulation-time scores. They are available for 99.7 % of stored games from the source already in use, at one extra request per finished game, and they remove the reason basketball is stuck at `mode: scrape` (the bookmaker settles on regulation time, production models final scores). The alternative, keeping final scores only, leaves a model that can say nothing about the 7.1 % of men's top-division games that are level after forty minutes.

## Your decisions

1.  **Direction.** v2 on R-INLA as the target for handball and basketball, with Stan kept as the weekly reference?
2.  **Shadow workflow.** May a new workflow fit v2 daily into a shadow tree? It adds R-INLA to CI and commits data to a new path; it does not touch live fits or published output.
3.  **Regulation-time scores.** Add two nullable columns and the game id to `results`, change the KKÍ ingest to fetch one game card per finished game, and backfill? This alters the ingest and a stored schema.
4.  **Men's handball draws.** Publish with the plain rounded margin (today's band), or switch the draw shift on at a shrunk value? The surplus of level scores is there, but it has not yet paid out of sample.
5.  **Home advantage on the site.** v2 has one home advantage per team for the margin. The published attack and defence components would be equal halves of it. Acceptable, or should the site show one number?
6.  **Regulation-time forecasts for basketball.** Publish them alongside the final-result forecast (a contract addition, needs a matching change in metill-platform), or keep them internal for now?
7.  **Package metadata.** The branch edits `DESCRIPTION`: five `Collate` entries for the new R files, added by `devtools::document()`. R-INLA is *not* yet declared in `Suggests` (its tests skip where it is missing), and it is not on CRAN, so declaring it also means an `Additional_repositories` entry and a pinned install in CI. Keep the Collate entries when the branch merges, and declare R-INLA now or only at cutover?

## Appendix

### Compute conditions

All fits ran on one M1 Pro (8 performance cores, 16 GB) shared with three other sessions fitting models. From 21:30 a shared limiter allowed at most two (later three) 4-core jobs at once; before that the machine was two to three times oversubscribed and swapping, and no wall time from that period is reported as a timing. Leapfrog counts, gradient counts and effective sample sizes do not depend on load. CmdStan 2.38.0 for every NUTS fit, R-INLA 25.6.7.

### Where each number comes from

Every number in this report is read from a result file under `/Users/brynjolfurjonsson/.claude-reviews/sports-hb-bb-v2/`. The table names the file and the fields behind each headline number; `docs/reports/2026-11-15-hb-bb-v2/check_headlines.R` recomputes them from exactly these fields without going through the report builder (its output: `logs/check_headlines.log`).

| Production sampler: sampled parameters, divergences, leapfrog steps, R-hat, ESS, wall time, machine slots | `out/res_<cell>_r0_prod.rds` | `$n_sampled`, `$n_divergent`, `$mean_leapfrog`, `$max_rhat`, `$worst_ess`, `$wall_secs`, `$machine` |
| Identified home advantage and the hyperparameter table of the v2 model; residual and mismatch tables; score variance / mean given strengths (the Poisson comparison) | `out/descriptives.rds` | `[[cell]]$hfa`, `$hyper_m`, `$hyper_t`, `$d` (one row per match with fitted means and residuals), `$by_div`, `$disp` (per division: `pearson_poisson` is score variance / mean, `binom_n55` the same against a binomial with 55 attacks) |
| Ladder tables: parameters, leapfrog, leave-one-out density, home advantage, held-out scores per rung; paired differences from production | `out/ladder.rds` (built from `out/res_<cell>_<rung>.rds`, `out/draws_<cell>_<rung>.rds`, `out/inla_validate_<cell>.rds`) | `$tab` (one row per cell and rung: `n_sampled`, `leapfrog`, `elpd`, `ha_mean`, `level_sd`, `ridge_cor`, `wall_secs`); `$scores[["<cell> <rung>"]]` (per held-out match: `ls_margin`, `ls_total`, `ll_wdl`) |
| R-INLA against Stan: hyperparameters, states, held-out predictor, log scores, leave-one-out | `out/compare_validation.rds` | `[["<cell> <response>"]]$hyper`, `$state`, `$pred`, `$log_score`, `$loo` |
| Within-season term at the fixed cutoff (sd, leave-one-out gain) | `out/inla_validate_<cell>.rds`, `out/ladder.rds` | `[["margin ar1 auto"]]$hyper_sd`, `$cpo` |
| Weekly-correlation sensitivity (0.90, 0.95, 0.98) | `out/within_rho.rds` | one row per cell and correlation: `loo`, `ls_margin` |
| Walk-forward predictions; seconds per cutoff (about 6 s, on the shared machine) | `out/wf_<cell>_none.rds` (handball; basketball trained on final scores), `out/wf_<cell>_none_reg.rds`, `out/wf_<cell>_ar1_reg.rds` | `$pred` (one row per predicted match: `mean_m`, `sd_m`, `sig2_m`, `mean_t`, `sd_t`, `sig2_t`); `$cut$secs_m + $cut$secs_t` |
| Walk-forward scores (3,930 matches); level-score shift, variance forms, Student-t, overtime; calibration by phase | `out/wf_scores.rds` | `[["<cell> none"]]$scores` (handball), `[["<cell> none_reg"]]$scores` (basketball): `lsm_*` margin, `lst_*` total, `ll_wdl_*` result, `ll_final_*` final result, `p_draw*`, `margin_fit`, `phase` |
| Within-season AR(1) minus static in the walk-forward (1,211 matches; 1. deild 549) | `out/wf_scores.rds` | `$within_j[["bb_m_reg"]]`, `[["bb_f_reg"]]`: `lsm_raw.ar1 - lsm_raw.static` and the same for `lst_raw`, `ll_wdl_raw` |
| Regulation-trained plus overtime against the final-score model | `out/wf_scores.rds` | `[["bb_m reg_vs_final"]]`, `[["bb_f reg_vs_final"]]`: `ll_final_shift_div - ll_wdl_raw.final`, `lsm_final_shift_div - lsm_raw.final` |
| v2 against production's stored forecasts (338 matches); mean expected margins; RMSE | `out/wf_compare.rds` | `[[cell]]$cmp`: production `ls_margin`, `ls_total`, `ll_wdl`, `mean_m.prod`; v2 `lsm_raw`, `lst_raw`, `ll_wdl_raw`, `mean_m.v2` |
| v2 and production against the Lengjan line | `out/wf_compare.rds` | `[[cell]]$market`: `ll_market`, `ll_v2`, `ll_prod` |
| Regulation-time coverage (99.7 %), overtime shares (7.1 % in men's Bónusdeild) | `kki/periods_matched.rds` (parsed cards: `kki/periods.tsv`, raw cards: `kki/raw/`) | one row per stored game: `ok`, `overtime`, `home_reg`, `away_reg`, `sex`, `division` |
| Run-to-run reproducibility of the R-INLA plug-in fits | `out/repro_descriptives.rds` (from the runs kept in `repro/run_*/out/descriptives.rds`) | `$fits` (per cell and response: `n_runs`, `n_modal`, `max_abs_fitted_diff`, `hyper_q50_modal`, `hyper_q50_other`), `$hfa` |
| Package tests | `logs/full_tests.log` | summary reporter output of `devtools::test()` |

Cells are `hb_m`, `hb_f`, `bb_m`, `bb_f`. The printed tables behind every section are also kept as text in `logs/`: `diag_prod.log`, `ladder_summary.log`, `compare_validation.log`, `wf_score.log`, `wf_compare.log`, `descriptives.log`, `kki_periods.log`.
